activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
story:
Florence spread the notebook page across the lunch table and pinned the corner with her milk carton before the breeze could invade the cafeteria and carry it off. On the page were two columns of numbers, game by game, for Lisa and for Issa.

"The tournament sheet is due to Mr. Ho tomorrow morning," Lisa said, tapping the deadline circled twice in red pen. "He only takes one of us as Florence's doubles partner. So make it fair."

Florence had watched both of them play basketball all season, and she had kept score in her notebook because arguments about who was better always turned into shouting. Now she added each column of points and divided by the number of games, twice, checking herself. Both averages came out the same. She slid the notebook to the middle of the table.

"You're identical," she said. "Eight points a game, both of you."

"That can't be right," Issa said. She leaned over the columns, her braid dropping into the milk puddle. "Look. Lisa scored eight every single game. Eight, eight, eight, like a robot. I had a sixteen, and a twenty, and then a two, and a zero." She pointed at the zero. "That was the day I twisted my ankle. And the two was the game right before the science trip, when I was up until one in the morning finishing my poster."

"Your poster," Florence said. "The one with the owl?"

" nocturnal animals, yes. Three weeks of work. I was a zombie at practice."

Florence looked at the columns again. Same total, same average, but Lisa's numbers sat in a tight line while Issa's leapt up and crashed down like a roller coaster she could almost hear. An average, she realized, squashed all those separate games into one number, and once it did, the shape of them disappeared. Two players could match on average and still be nothing alike.

"Here's what I keep thinking," she said slowly. "In the tournament, we play four matches in one day. Whoever I pick has to show up four times in a row."

Issa sat back. "So you're picking Lisa."

"I didn't say that." Florence pulled out a pencil. "I said I want to test something. Tomorrow morning, before the sheet is due, both of you shoot twenty free throws. Not one average score. I write down every single shot, each one, in order."

Lisa frowned. "Why does the order matter?"

"Because I want to see the spread," Florence said. "I want to see whether you go make, make, make, or miss, miss, hot streak, collapse. One number can't tell me that."

The next morning the gym smelled like floor wax, and Mr. Ho unlocked the door at seven fifteen and watched from the bleachers with his coffee, saying nothing. Lisa shot first: fifteen makes out of twenty, evenly spaced, steady as rain dripping off a gutter. Then Issa, rested and ankle taped, hit her first nine in a row, missed five straight, and finished with six more makes. Florence wrote down every shot.

"Same count," Lisa said, counting the marks. "Fifteen each."

Florence ran her finger down Issa's column, over the cold streak in the middle. "You're the better pick when you're hot, and the worse pick when you're not," she said. "And I can't know which one walks onto the court."

Issa bounced the ball once, twice. "So it's Lisa?"

Lisa picked up the pen and turned the sign-up sheet toward them. "Write both our names in the alternates line," she said. "Florence picks her partner the morning of the tournament, game by game, and I shoot first."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
story:
Dominic sat at the library table with the shoe magazine open in front of him, though he was supposed to be finishing his homework. On the page, the basketball star Marcus Hale stood on a court, pointing at the sneakers on his feet. The headline read, "The best shoe in the game." Dominic had read the page four times. The sneakers cost more than any pair he had ever owned, and his birthday was in three weeks.

Dastan dropped into the chair across from him and looked at the magazine. "Those are the Marcus Hales. Ines has a cousin who has them. Half the team at my old school had them too." He tapped the page. "Everyone's getting them."

"Everyone," Dominic repeated. He turned the page. There was a full-page spread showing twenty kids at a bus stop, all wearing the same sneakers, with the words "Join the millions" printed across the top. Dominic frowned at it. Somehow the picture made the shoes seem even better, and he noticed that it did that without saying anything about the shoes at all.

He got up and found Ms. Fitzgerald at the reference desk. "Do you have anything about how ads work?" he asked. She led him to a shelf and pulled out a thin book called How They Persuade You. Back at the table, he opened it and started reading. One section was called "The Testimonial." He read it twice, then looked up.

"It's called a testimonial," he told Dastan, holding up the book. "It's when they use somebody famous to say a product is good. But the person might not know anything special about it, and they might be getting paid." Dastan leaned over to read the page himself. "So Marcus Hale gets paid to wear them?" Dominic shrugged. "Maybe. Maybe not. The book says you can't tell from the ad."

He decided to test it. At the computer station he typed Marcus Hale's name and the sneaker brand together. The first result was a news story from two years earlier: the brand had signed a deal with Hale worth millions, and after that he wore their shoes in every game. Dominic read the number twice to calibrate his expectations; a paid deal that big meant the shoes were a job, not a choice. He clicked back to the brand's own site and found a smaller item, a quote from the team's equipment manager saying the shoes were versatile enough for guards and centers alike. That was a person whose whole job was knowing shoes, and he had chosen a plain word, not a headline.

Dominic copied the page numbers onto his hand and walked back to the table. Ines had arrived and was looking at the magazine. "Those are so cool," she said. "Marcus Hale wears them."

"He gets paid to wear them," Dominic said. He slid the book across the table to her. "Page twelve."

story:
Arthur had been counting down to the farm field trip for two weeks, and when the bus finally rattled up the gravel drive, he was first out the door. Krish and Jia followed, both squinting in the glare of a sun that had turned the morning into something like an oven. Mr. Mercer clapped his hands and announced the plan: a tour of the barns, then the pig pens, and everyone had to be back at the bus by noon, because the driver had another route at one.

The pig pens came last, and they were a mess. Every pig was caked in brown mud, lying in shallow wallows or trudging through the slop with what Arthur considered terrible manners. "They're just dirty," Krish said, wrinkling his nose. "Our bus smells better than this." Jia laughed, but Arthur frowned, because something about it didn't fit. The pens had clean, shaded spots under the roof, and the water trough was full. If the pigs only wanted to be dirty, why had two of them squeezed into the same tiny wallow instead of spreading out into all that space?

He crouched by the fence and watched. The mud in the wallows was wet and dark, while the dirt by the trough had baked pale and cracked. He put his hand near the fence line, felt heat radiating off the dry ground, and a thought clicked into place. "It's the mud itself," he said. "They're not choosing filth. Look, the wet spots are the coolest places in the whole pen." Jia crouched beside him and touched the fence rail. "It's like a hot iron," she agreed.

The farmer came by with a bucket, and Arthur asked whether the pigs rolled in mud to cool down. The farmer nodded and said that was exactly it, since pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days. Arthur felt his ears go hot with something better than embarrassment. "I thought they were just gross," Krish admitted. "Okay, I officially changed my mind. They're engineers."

Mr. Mercer checked his watch and called that they had ten minutes to integrate back into their groups and head for the bus. Arthur, always meticulous about observations, made one last test: he tossed a splash of trough water into a corner of the dry pen. The smallest pig lifted its head, waddled over, and flopped into the damp patch with a grunt of pure satisfaction. The sun climbed toward its noon plateau above the barn roof, and Arthur jogged for the bus, grinning the whole way. "Told you," he said to Krish. "Smartest dirty animals on this farm."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
The ferry to Sandpoint Island left at nine sharp, and the ranger's tide pool tour began at nine thirty, which gave Easton exactly twenty minutes to solve a problem: his friend Haris was turning green on the bench beside him. "It's the wobble," Haris said, gripping the rail. "The whole boat wobbles." Easton knew that feeling. Last summer, on the lake ferry back home, he had spent the whole crossing with his head between his knees while his little sister munched crackers above him. He had sworn he would never be that kid again, and now here was Haris being that kid instead.

"Last year I felt exactly like you," Easton said. "I tried crackers, I tried closing my eyes, nothing worked. Then I stood up and looked at the far shore, and it just... eased off. I don't know why. I was staring at one fixed point, way out where nothing moves." Haris looked at him like he was making it up, but the ferry heaved again and Haris swallowed hard. "Worth a try," he croaked.

They pushed through the cabin door onto the open deck. Other passengers huddled near the snack bar, where a handwritten sign said CASH ONLY, and a boy was trading loose coins for a candy bar because bills were useless currency out here, the card reader having died weeks ago. Easton led Haris to the bow and pointed straight ahead, past the rail, past the whitecaps, to where the shoreline of the mainland lay stretched out flat and steady. "Don't watch the water going by," Easton said. "Watch the horizon. That's what I did. Fixed distant point. Just keep your eyes there."

Haris fixed his eyes there. The ferry rocked, the deck tilted, and Haris's knees bent to catch his balance, but he kept staring at the far shore. Slowly the green drained out of his face. His grip on the rail loosened. "It's working," he said, sounding amazed. "How does staring at the horizon help? It's like my eyes and my ears finally agree with each other." Easton shrugged, because that was honestly all he understood too, but it was enough.

The island grew closer, all dark rock and wind-bent pines clinging to what the park brochure called an impoverished patch of soil, too thin for much to grow except those tough little trees. The tour group was already gathering at the dock, and the ranger, Ms. Shapiro, was waving them over. Easton grabbed Haris's sleeve. "Come on, we can still make it." Haris took one last look at the flat line of the mainland, then turned and ran with him down the gangplank, both of them sprinting across the dock toward Ms. Shapiro and the waiting crowd, the ferry horn blaring behind them.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
Keira sat cross-legged on the grass behind her house, her sketchbook propped against a lawn chair, and stared at the empty page. On Saturday she had stood at the corner of Maple and Third with her friend Ameera, both of them trying to draw the street with one vanishing point, the way Ms. Pierre had shown them in art class. Every line was supposed to run toward that single dot on the page. But Keira's drawing kept coming out crooked, the buildings leaning like they were about to topple into the road. Ameera's looked even worse. "Maybe we're just bad at this," Ameera had said, shoving her pencil back in her bag.

Keira refused to believe that. In class, using one vanishing point had worked perfectly. She flipped back through her sketchbook to the drawing she'd done of the hallway outside the art room, and there it was: clean, straight, the lockers shrinking toward one dot. So the technique wasn't the problem. Something was different about the corner, and she meant to figure out what.

First she tested the simplest idea she had. She folded the corner drawing in half and held it up beside the hallway drawing, comparing where the lines met. In the hallway drawing, every line crashed together at one point. In the corner drawing, the lines on the left side of the street wandered toward one spot and the lines on the right side wandered toward another. It wasn't one point at all. It was two. Her hand, not her brain, had known something was wrong.

That night she texted Soleil, who lived on a long straight road. "Can you do me a favor?" she wrote. "Stand in the middle of your street facing straight down it. Not at a corner. Just straight. Then tell me what the fronts of the houses look like." Soleil wrote back: "Weird request but ok. They're all facing me. Like the flat fronts are pointed right at me, and the sides sort of shrink away. It looks kind of desolate actually, like the road is swallowing everything into one little dot far away." Keira read the message three times, then grinned at her ceiling.

On Sunday afternoon she set up her sketchbook in the backyard again and called Ameera. "I was wrong about the corner," Keira said when she arrived. "You weren't bad at it. The corner was bad at it." Ameera frowned. "What does that mean?" Keira tapped the folded drawings. "One vanishing point works when you face straight down a street. At the corner we were facing two streets at once, so the drawing needed something else." She dismantled her old attempt, erasing line after line until only the ghost of the corner remained, then drew a fresh horizon and a single dot on it. "Your street, Soleil's street. Straight ahead, fronts facing us, everything running back to one point. Try it."

Ameera sat down in the grass, took out her pencil, and set her dot. "Ready?" she said. "Ready," Keira said, and they both began to draw.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
story:
The automatic doors hissed open, and Vincent walked in holding his crumpled list like it was a treasure map. He was there for a school project: Ms. Patel had told the class to explain which was riskier, a stock or a bond, and she had suggested comparing them somewhere real. A grocery store, she said, full of companies trying to earn your money, was as real as it got. Vincent was not sure how a shelf of cereal was supposed to teach him anything, but he had a plan anyway.

Near the cereal aisle he found Amira and Davina, who had been dumped at the store while Amira's mom shopped. "Perfect," Vincent said. "You two are my hypothetical investors. Amira, you own stock in this cereal company. Davina, you own its bonds."

"I don't even know what a bond is," Davina said, tossing a box of oat squares back onto the shelf.

"That's the point. Neither do I, really." He pulled out his notebook. "Ms. Patel said a stock is a tiny piece of the company, so if it does badly, your piece is worth less and they can cut your dividend whenever they want. I looked it up last night." He tapped his pen. "A dividend is money the company pays you just for holding the stock. And a bond is basically you lending the company money, and they promise to pay you interest."

Amira picked up the box again. "So if the company has a bad year and stops paying me my dividend, that's allowed?"

"That's what the article said. Companies can cut or skip dividends."

Davina frowned. "But they promised."

"That's what irritates me too," Vincent admitted. "But here's the thing I found. If they miss a promised interest payment on a bond, that's called a default. That's serious. Dividends can just vanish and nobody calls it anything."

"So the bond is safer," Amira said slowly, like she was testing a rope bridge. "Even though it's the same company."

"Same company, different promise." Vincent wrote it down. In the context of his blank page, that one sentence suddenly looked like the whole answer. The stock was riskier because its payments could be cut or skipped without a word for it, while the bond's payment, if missed, was a default.

Then a voice behind them said, "Are you three analyzing my store?" It was Ms. Patel herself, holding a basket of eggs, wearing her weekend jacket instead of her teaching cardigan. Vincent froze. Assignments were not supposed to follow you into cereal aisles.

She glanced at his notebook, and a small smile crossed her face. "Dividends can be cut. Missed bond interest is a default. Whoever taught you that?"

"You did," Vincent said. "Sort of. Yesterday. It just took a shelf of oat squares to make it stick."

Ms. Patel set her eggs in the basket. "Then write it up. And Vincent, buy the oat squares. You owe them that much."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Bennett raced along platform four so fast his backpack bounced like a second heartbeat. His grandfather was arriving on the 3:40, and Bennett had the whole week planned: model rockets on Saturday, the science museum on Tuesday, and tonight, chili dogs. When the train doors slid open with a hiss, Grandpa stepped out holding a duffel bag and a paper cup of tea that had gone cold somewhere outside the city.

"There he is," Grandpa boomed, and Bennett grinned so wide his cheeks ached. On the drive home, though, Bennett noticed things. Grandpa kept his coat zipped all the way up, even with the heater running. His hands, when he pointed at a billboard, looked pale, almost translucent in the late light, like paper held up to a window. And at the house, Grandpa settled into the recliner in the den, the coldest room in the whole place, without saying a single word about it. That was the part that bothered Bennett most. Grandpa would complain about the referee, about the price of licorice, about Bennett's shoelaces. Not about cold.

At school the next morning, Bennett leaned across the lab table toward Jensen. "Do old people get cold differently?" Jensen shrugged, but Gracie, who was sorting index cards, looked up. "My aunt's a nurse. She says older adults are at greater risk of hypothermia than younger adults. That's a dangerous drop in body temperature. Her unit treats somebody every winter." Bennett repeated the word under his breath. Hypothermia. Grandpa, sitting calm and quiet in a chilly room, not complaining. He had a theory, and he knew exactly how to test it.

That afternoon he borrowed the classroom thermometer from Ms. Robinson, promising to return it by Friday. At home, he set it on the den table, watched Grandpa do the crossword, and wrote down the reading every twenty minutes. Sixty-three degrees, then sixty-two. Grandpa said nothing. Bennett's stomach tightened. He marched to the thermostat and cranked it up, then dragged a space heater beside the recliner and draped his own fleece blanket over Grandpa's knees like he was tucking in a king.

Grandpa lowered the crossword. "What's all this?" Bennett exhaled, then explained about Gracie's aunt, about hypothermia, about the readings in his notebook, his voice getting faster as he went. Grandpa was quiet for a moment, and Bennett braced for teasing. Instead Grandpa said, "Sixty-two, huh? No wonder my tea kept going cold." Then came the twist: he pulled his phone from his pocket and held it up. On the screen was a note titled BENNETT'S WEEK, and item one said, Let the kid fuss over me a little. "Your grandmother told me you'd been studying up," Grandpa said. "She said, 'He'll figure it out. He always does.'"

Bennett laughed until he had to sit on the arm of the couch. Then he grabbed a second blanket, because even a scheming grandfather deserved two, and announced, "Chili dogs. Kitchen. Five minutes."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
The deadline was Sunday morning, and it was already Thursday night when Willow stood in her grandmother's kitchen holding a photocopied booklet like it might bite her. In three days she would stand among the adults at the Gurdwara and recite Japji Sahib from memory as part of her preparation for Amrit Sanchar, and so far she could get through about four lines before her brain went blank.

"You are chewing your lip again," her grandmother said, sliding a cup of chai across the counter. "That habit is toxic to your concentration."

Willow laughed despite herself. "Everything is toxic to my concentration. The words all sound the same when I panic. Ek onkar satnam, karta purakh, and then static." She flipped the pages, forty stanzas of Gurmukhi she could read slowly but not yet hold in her head.

Her cousin Otis wandered in from the living room, headphones around his neck. "Why does it have to be this prayer, anyway? Why not something short?"

"Because it's recited at Amrit Sanchar," their grandmother said simply, and went back to stirring the pot. "That is the Khalsa initiation ceremony. When you take amrit, Japji Sahib is part of it. So you learn it before, and you learn it well."

Willow stared at the booklet. She had known the ceremony was coming, known she was nervous about it, but she hadn't connected the two things until that moment. The morning prayer wasn't just homework her grandmother had invented. It was the same words that would be spoken during the initiation itself, which meant that every line she learned now would be waiting for her there, already inside her, like friends in a room she hadn't entered yet. Otis saw her face change and raised an eyebrow, but she just said, "I need your phone."

She had an idea she wanted to test. Instead of staring at the page, she recorded herself reading one stanza, played it back while walking the length of the hallway and back, then tried to say it before listening again. One stanza, ten laps. Her grandmother watched from the kitchen doorway as Willow muttered and stumbled and restarted. "You look like a pigeon," Otis said, and Willow threw a cushion at him without breaking her rhythm.

By Friday night she had eight stanzas. On Saturday she noticed something: the booklet's page had a symmetry to it, the way certain phrases returned in mirrored places across stanzas, and once she saw the pattern, whole chunks locked together like puzzle pieces. When a line slipped away from her at the sink on Sunday morning, she stopped, walked seven steps the way she had practiced, and the words came back on their own.

At the Gurdwara, standing with the others while Japji Sahib rose around her, she found she did not have to grab for the lines. They sustained her, carrying her forward while her heart pounded, all the way to the final stanza.

Afterward Otis found her in the hallway. "So? Did you get through it?"

Willow held up the worn booklet. "Forty stanzas, ten hallway laps each," she said. "You owe me four hundred laps of pigeon-watching."

story:
Ivy set the greeting card on the picnic table and pressed the fold with her thumb. The thick card cracked along the crease in a jagged white line, and the paint on the outside flaked off in little chips, like frost. It was the third card she had ruined that afternoon. Her mother's birthday was tomorrow, and the folded cards in the craft store would cost more than the money in her jar.

She sat on the back step and thought about last winter, when Edmond's father had rebuilt the fence. Edmond had watched him work and told Ivy about it later, laughing at his own memory of it. His father had run a tool along each plank before bending it around the fence post, a dull-edged thing pressed in a straight line, and the wood had folded smooth as bread dough instead of splintering. Ivy had not understood it then, but the picture stayed in her head.

Maybe card worked like that too. She went back to the table, where the lawn smelled of cut grass and the ice in her lemonade had melted to a thin ring. She found a butter knife with a rounded, worn edge, laid a ruler across the card, and drew the blunt tool along the line once, firmly, like a piston moving in a single steady stroke. Then she folded the card. The crease came out clean and straight, with no cracks and no bumpy lumps along the fold. She ran her finger over it and grinned.

"That's the one," she said out loud.

Jayden leaned over the fence a few minutes later, chin on his arms. "Why is yours flat and the other ones all ugly?"

"You score it first," Ivy said. "You run a blunt tool along the line before you fold, and the fold comes out straight instead of cracked."

Jayden squinted at the ruined cards in the grass, then at the new one. "Huh. That's actually kind of great." He pointed at her paint set. "Can you do a lily on it? Mom likes lilies." Ivy revised her plan for the front of the card, sketching lightly in pencil before she touched the brush to it. The petals came out the way she wanted, soft and a little crooked, but right.

By evening the card stood finished on the kitchen counter, propped against the sugar bowl, folded edge crisp as a book's spine. Ivy's mother came in from the garden with dirt on her hands and saw it there. She picked it up, opened it slowly along the clean crease, and read the words inside twice.

"You made this?" her mother asked.

"All by myself," Ivy said. "Every fold of it."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
story:
Felix stood on Ibraheem's porch with a folded note in his hand, breathing in the smell of rain that had rolled through an hour ago. The grass was lush and dripping, and mist still hung over the backyard like slow-moving vapor. He had written the note last night, after the fight, and now he had to actually give it to someone.

The fight was with Brynlee. On Tuesday he had knocked her volcano project off the lab table, laughed with Ibraheem about the mess, and then told everyone in the cafeteria that she had overreacted. She hadn't spoken to him since. He wanted his best friend back, and the note was his plan.

Inside, Ibraheem was spreading clay across a cardboard base, building his own model for Mr. Levy's class. "You came," he said. "Sit down. Tell me what that is."

"It's an apology," Felix said. He unfolded it and read it out loud. "Brynlee, I'm sorry if you got upset about the volcano thing."

Ibraheem set down his clay tool. "Read that again." Felix did. "Sorry if you got upset. That's weird. It makes it sound like it's her fault for being upset, not yours for knocking it over."

Felix read it a third time, slower. He was starting to see what Ibraheem meant, like noticing a pattern hidden in a sentence he had already checked twice. "My sister watched this video," Ibraheem said, rolling a ridge of clay. "She said that's called a non-apology. It's sorry about your feelings, not sorry about what you did." Felix copied the word onto his palm with a finger, then hunted through his backpack for a pen.

"So the note's not really an apology at all," he said. "It's a fake one." He spread the paper flat on the table, next to Ibraheem's half-built mountain, and crossed out his old line. The pen tore through once and he smoothed the page and started over on the back.

He tried writing it out several ways. "I'm sorry your project broke" still blamed the project. "I'm sorry the accident happened" blamed the accident. Finally he wrote, "I'm sorry I knocked over your volcano and laughed. That was my fault, both parts." He read it aloud, and it felt different in his mouth, harder to say and more true.

"Better," Ibraheem said, but then he pinched off a piece of clay and illustrated the problem with it, squashing it flat under his thumb. "Except you laughed about it with me, at lunch, in front of everyone. The note fixes Tuesday morning, not Tuesday lunch."

Felix stared at the flattened clay. He had been thinking about the volcano and forgetting the cafeteria completely, like a person who fixes one broken window in a house and ignores the hole in the roof. "Then I go say it there," he said. "Where I did it."

They found Brynlee at her locker before first period. Felix held out the note, but he didn't hand it over, because he wanted her to hear the words from him. "I'm sorry I knocked over your volcano and laughed," he said. "That was my fault, both parts. I'm sorry I did it in front of everyone, too."

Brynlee looked at the paper, then at him. "That's a real apology," she said. "Not a sorry-if one." She slung her backpack over her shoulder. "You can help me rebuild the lava flow at lunch. It takes two hands anyway."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
story:
Ellie stood at the kitchen counter with a slice of toast she couldn't eat. Tomorrow was the piano recital, and her heart was pounding so hard she could feel it in her throat. Her hands shook when she picked up her water glass. She pressed her palm against her forehead. No fever, but something was wrong with her. She wondered if she should tell her mom she was too sick to perform.

Instead she sat down, took out her phone, and texted Damian, whose older brother was something of a veteran at recitals and auditions. "My heart is going crazy and my hands are shaking. Am I getting sick?" Damian replied three minutes later: "No. When the brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing quicker." Then a second message: "It's called the fight-or-flight response. Your body thinks the recital is a bear." A third: "Unless you actually see a bear at the recital, in which case, cancel."

Ellie laughed, which felt strange with her heart still hammering. So her body wasn't broken. It was doing a job, just the wrong one. She decided to test it. If adrenaline was making her breathing quick, maybe slow breathing could signal that things were fine. She set a timer for two minutes, sat up straight in the kitchen chair, and breathed in for four counts and out for six. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four, five, six. Halfway through, her shoulders dropped. By the end of the timer, her hands were steadier, and her heart no longer felt like a drum solo.

She found a sticky note and wrote herself a plan: breathe before bed, no screens after eight, lights out by nine, and repeat the breathing in the morning. Sleep mattered too. She had read that a tired brain felt more vulnerable to stress, and tomorrow she did not want her brain mistaking an audience of parents for a pack of wolves. She stuck the note on the refrigerator under a magnet shaped like a pineapple.

The next evening, Ellie stood backstage with her sheet music. Her heart picked up speed, exactly as predicted. Grandma Ruth arrived on Sunday with one suitcase and a bag of mint candies, and by Tuesday Sydney had figured out something odd. At the kitchen table, Grandma caught every word, even when Sydney mumbled. But in the backyard, while the sprinkler hissed across the grass, Grandma kept tipping her head and saying, "Say that again, dear?" Sydney wanted the week to go well, so she decided to find the pattern.

At first she blamed herself. Maybe she was talking too fast out there, or standing too far away. So she tried an experiment on Wednesday. She stood at the same distance from Grandma in both places and said the same sentence at the same speed. In the quiet kitchen, Grandma laughed at the joke about Ms. Ricci's runaway chalk. In the backyard, with the neighbor's leaf blower roaring, Grandma only smiled and nodded, and Sydney could tell she hadn't caught a thing.

That was a clue. It wasn't the words and it wasn't Sydney. Something invisible was changing. She thought about the sprinkler, the leaf blower, the crows that argued in the maple every morning. She remembered the airport in the summer, how Grandma had gone silent for the whole layover even though she'd been chatty at home on the porch. Sydney had assumed Grandma was tired back then. Now it seemed more probable that the noise was the problem, not the words and not the tiredness.

On Thursday she tested it. She invited Aurora and Sulaiman over, and they planned a backyard picnic. Sulaiman wanted the portable speaker on. Sydney said no, and when he asked why, she said, "Grandma's hearing, it's the background noise that gets her." Then Sydney did the opposite of the usual plan: she moved the picnic to the far corner of the yard, away from the sprinkler line, and asked her dad to hold off on the mower. Aurora brought a quilt and they all sat close, in a tight little circle.

It worked. Grandma told them about her own grandmother, who had crossed an ocean with two spoons and a photograph, and how every descendant in the family still made her jam recipe wrong. She told a story about nearly submerging a canoe at summer camp, and Sulaiman laughed so hard he fell off the quilt. Sydney watched her grandma's face, quick and bright, no more nodding and smiling through guesses.

Later, when the sprinklers clicked on and Grandma's replies went vague again, Sydney stood up and turned the timer dial until the water stopped. Grandma raised her eyebrows.

"Rain check," Sydney said, "for the grass."

"So write it like that," said Alys. "If... then. Prediction, not a wish."

story:
Emile had one job during spring break: sit quietly in his mom's office until five o'clock. He had failed at it within forty minutes, mostly because the stapler was fascinating and the supply closet was full of rubber bands. His mom walked over, set her coffee down, and pointed at her computer. "You want something to do? Learn this. Make a spreadsheet that adds a column and turns it into a bar chart."

"Sure," Emile said, which was his standard answer to things he had never done.

He opened a new file and typed numbers into a column: how many rubber bands, staples, and paperclips he had counted in the supply closet. Then he got stuck. The sum kept coming out wrong. He typed =SUM(A2:A7) and got a number that made no sense, 42, when he knew the total was 58. He stared at the screen, then called Hargun, who was home and, according to Hargun, a spreadsheet genius because his dad was an accountant.

"Read me your numbers," Hargun said. "Start at the top."

"D4 has 12," Emile read, squinting at the column. He went down the list. Hargun did the math out loud and got 58, which was exactly what Emile wanted and exactly what the spreadsheet refused to say.

"So the formula's wrong," Hargun said. "Wait, why are you in D4? Your numbers should be in column A if you started at the left."

Emile looked again. His numbers weren't in column A at all. Somewhere along the way he had clicked one column over, and his list was sitting in D while the formula summed A. He laughed so loudly that a man in the next cubicle peeked over the wall like a suspicious prairie dog.

"C4 is the cell in column C, row 4," Emile said slowly, following the letters across the top and the numbers down the side with his finger. "So D4 is column D, row four. The address is the letter first, then the number."

"A spreadsheet genius would have known that," Hargun admitted.

"You're a spreadsheet genius the way I'm a quiet office kid." Emile fixed the formula to =SUM(D2:D7), and the number 58 appeared like a magic trick he had performed on himself. He highlighted the labels and the totals, clicked the bar chart button, and three bars sprang up, the rubber band one towering over the others like a monument to boredom.

He screenshotted it and sent it to his mom with the message "I persisted." She wrote back one word: "Impressive." Then she sent a second message: "Now do the same thing for my budget, and don't touch column C."

Emile looked at column C, which was labeled Petty Cash and looked extremely vulnerable.

"Okay," he said to the screen. "Let's talk about your secrets."

story:
Benjamin slid his copy of the story across the desk so Brynn could see the page. "It's called The Most Dangerous Game," he said. "By Richard Connell. Written in 1924. Mr. Fitzgerald wants us to find what the writer hints at before it happens."

"So it's a scavenger hunt," Brynn said. "But for clues in a story."

Kiana leaned over from the next row. "The whole first page is a guy on a yacht. Nothing happens."

Benjamin read the opening again anyway. He stopped at one line and put his finger under it. "Listen. The sailors are scared of this island. Whitney says even the tough old crew feels dread when they pass it. And it has a name."

"What kind of name?" Kiana asked.

"Ship-Trap Island."

Brynn sat up. "Wait. That's the name of the place? Ship-Trap Island?"

"That's what it says." Benjamin turned the book so she could read it herself. He copied the words onto his worksheet and looked at them. A ship. A trap. An island that traps ships. He thought about the turbulent water around it, the dark night, the sailors' dread. The writer had put the danger right in the name of the place before the main character even arrived.

"So the name is doing something," he said slowly. "It's like a sign on a door that says Do Not Enter. The characters sail right past the sign and go in anyway."

"Then the story is telling us what's coming," Kiana said, "and the people in it don't notice."

Mr. Fitzgerald walked between the rows, checking worksheets. He stopped at Benjamin's desk and read the line Benjamin had underlined. "And what does that suggest to you?"

"The sailors' fear and the name mean there's danger waiting on that island," Benjamin said. "The writer gives it away before we get there. It hints at what's going to happen."

"Put that in your paragraph," Mr. Fitzgerald said. He moved on to the next row.

At lunch Benjamin tested his idea out loud, because saying it a different way would show him if he actually believed it. "Imagine the island had a tenant," he said, dipping a fry in ketchup. "Someone living there who set the trap on purpose. The name of the island is basically the story whispering that the trap exists."

Brynn nodded. "You could accompany Rainsford there in the story and still miss it, because he misses it. He falls off the yacht."

"He falls off the yacht," Kiana agreed, "and swims toward the place everyone else is afraid of."

Benjamin wrote his paragraph that night at the kitchen table, quoting the exact name and the sailors' dread, explaining that both hinted at the danger waiting there. He read it once out loud to check that it made sense. Then he put his pencil down and turned back to the last page of the story.

"He's at the door of the chateau," Benjamin said to the empty kitchen. "Knock, knock."

Abigail smoothed her dress for the third time and stared at the gift in her lap. Her mother's old college friend Sunee was getting married, and the invitation had said the ceremony would blend Thai and American traditions. Abigail only knew one thing about Thai weddings, which was nothing. In the hotel ballroom, gold garlands hung from the ceiling, and a table near the door held a mountain of wrapped boxes in silver and white. She put hers, a set of painted bowls, near the top and hoped it was the approximate right thing, because she'd guessed at it entirely.

She found Sheldon by the buffet, already holding a plate piled with rice and something that smelled like lime and chili. "Watch," he whispered, nodding toward the door. An older woman was greeting guests with her palms pressed together at her chest, fingers under her chin, and a small bow. Every Thai guest returned the same gesture. Abigail's intuition told her there was a rule here, a pattern she couldn't see written anywhere, so she decided to test it. When Sunee's grandmother drifted toward them, Abigail pressed her palms together and bowed slightly. The grandmother's whole face lit up, and she bowed back even lower.

At the tables, the rules kept multiplying. Sheldon reached across three place settings for the satay, and a boy about eight years old gave him a look that could have frozen the chili sauce. Abigail filed that away too: in this family, reaching was worse than asking.

The trouble came after the toasts. A little flower girl, maybe four years old, fell asleep in a chair with her shoes kicked off, and Abigail's mother's friend from work, a cheerful man named Dan, leaned over to pat the child's hair before carrying her to her parents. Abigail grabbed his wrist. "Don't," she said, a little too loud. Heads turned. "The head is sacred," she said, quieter now, her heart pounding because she was only repeating what the grandmother had murmured to her a minute earlier, smiling, after Abigail had asked about the flower girl's tiny gold crown. "Even patting a kid's head can be rude."

Dan stepped back with his hands raised, and for a second Abigail thought she had ruined the wedding. Then the grandmother appeared at her elbow, patted her own shoulder in invitation, and guided her toward the dessert table, where sticky rice mango sat in little banana leaves. "You listen well," the grandmother said, pressing a second helping into Abigail's hands. Behind them, the flower girl stirred, blinked, and reached sleepily for her gold crown.

story:
The nature trail behind school had three benches, one wasp nest, and today, thanks to Ms. Nasser, twenty-two kids carrying field microscopes in foam cases. Christopher balanced his case on his knee at the second bench and peeled a paper-thin layer off the onion he'd been told to bring from home. His worksheet had three boxes to fill: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. He could see the wall fine, a tidy brick pattern like a garden fence, and the nucleus showed up as a small dark dot. The membrane was nowhere.

"It's invisible," he told Sky, who had the bench spot next to him and had so far drawn what looked like a map of an empty parking lot.

"It's there. It's just pressed right against the wall, so you can't tell them apart." Sky leaned over his eyepiece. "Maybe if something pulled it away from the wall you'd see it. Like pulling a curtain off a fence."

Christopher considered this. He had a water bottle, a packet of trail mix, and a small tube of salt from his lunch, which he'd brought for his tomatoes. He nudged the tomatoes aside and thought about the salt. He'd seen his dad sprinkle salt on slugs, back when they had a garden, and the slugs had sort of shriveled. If salt did something like that to a cell, the inside might shrink while the wall stayed put.

He mixed a pinch of salt with a few drops of water from his bottle, dripped it onto the edge of his slide, and watched through the eyepiece. Nothing. Then something. The lining of each cell began to peel inward, a thin dark edge shrinking away from the wall like a deflating balloon inside a box.

"Oh," Christopher said. "There it is."

"Where?" Sky shoved in beside him, which irritated Christopher slightly, since one eyepiece really fit only one head, but he slid over anyway. Sky went quiet for a long moment. "It's the membrane. You can actually label it now."

Ms. Nasser came down the trail, checking worksheets as she walked, and stopped at their bench. She looked at Christopher's drawing, where the three labels sat in confident pencil, and raised an eyebrow at the salt tube and the wet slide.

"Who taught you about plasmolysis?" she asked.

"Is that what this is called?" Christopher said. "Nobody taught me. I had tomatoes."

Ms. Nasser looked at Sky's worksheet, which still showed the empty parking lot, then back at the slide. "Then you'd better draw it before it wears off. And Sky, take notes." She moved on down the trail, pausing only to warn a boy near bench three that a wasp attack was imminent if he kept poking the nest with a stick.

Sky borrowed the salt and made her own drop, and after two misses and one drowned slide she got it too, the thin membrane pulling inward in every cell at once. She labeled hers with a flourish and added a fourth label nobody had asked for: "plasmolysis, discovered by Christopher and his tomatoes."

Christopher started to say he hadn't discovered anything, that people probably knew this already, and then decided against it. He peeled a fresh layer of onion, laid it flat in a drop of plain water, and watched the membrane fade back against the wall like it had never left.

"Guess it only shows up when it's shrinking," he said, and reached for the salt again.

story:
Scarlett logged into the game lobby right after dinner and found Callan already there, his username glowing in the chat window. The lobby was loud in the way online lobbies always were: half the players typing in all capitals about a tournament, the other half whispering in private messages so quiet you'd never know they existed unless you were one of them.

"You deleted it," Callan typed in their private channel. "The whole clan page post. Gone."

"I know," Scarlett typed back. Last week she had written a long public announcement claiming she could beat anyone in the lobby using only a wooden spoon as her controller metaphor, which had made sense at midnight and no sense at all by morning. Marc-Antoine had screenshotted it before she deleted it, which was bad enough. But then Mr. Rossi, their teacher, had mentioned something in passing that stuck in her head like a burr. He had said, "The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages." A trillion. She hadn't known that was even a number you could apply to web pages.

"So it's gone," Callan repeated.

"Maybe not," she typed. "Mr. Rossi said the Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages. If it saved our clan page, my post might still be in there." She opened a second browser tab while Callan sent back a single row of question marks. She typed the clan page address into the Wayback Machine's search bar and waited, her chair creaking as she leaned forward.

A list of old snapshots appeared. She clicked the one from two days before her deletion, and there it was: her post, word for word, wooden spoon and all. She copied the link and pasted it into the private channel. For a moment nothing happened. Then Callan sent a string of laughing emotes so long it filled the whole window.

"Marc-Antoine," she typed, switching to the public channel, where her message appeared for everyone in the lobby to see, in full view, no privacy at all. That was the thing about public and private she was starting to understand: the public channel was like shouting in a gym, the private one like a note passed under a desk. She had put her embarrassing post in the gym.

Marc-Antoine's reply came fast. "You found the archived copy before I could send it. I was going to be diplomatic about it. Like a diplomat. Very smooth."

"You were going to commute my sentence?" she typed.

"That's not what commute means," Callan wrote privately. "Commuting a sentence means reducing a punishment."

"Fine," she typed publicly. "Then here's the deal. The archived post says I can beat anyone with a wooden spoon. I can't take it back, apparently, so I'm just going to say it in here: I approximate the skills of a wooden spoon, and I'm proud."

The lobby chat filled with laughing players, and Marc-Antoine sent her a trade request for an actual wooden spoon skin, priced at one coin.

"Deal," she typed, and clicked accept.

story:
Nevaeh stood at the kitchen counter with the biggest knife her mom would allow, an onion, and a printed recipe she'd found on a cooking site. The recipe had been posted by someone anonymous, just a username with a pot emoji, but hundreds of people had commented that the sauce was better than anything from a jar. That was her objective for the evening: chop the onion, build the sauce from scratch, and serve it over pasta before her little brother started whining about being hungry.

First she had to survive the onion. Her eyes were already stinging from the first cut, and her grip felt clumsy. She curled her fingers on the onion like claws, knuckles forward, so the blade could only bump against bone instead of fingertips. It was slower than she expected. The pieces came out uneven, some thin as paper, some fat as dice, and she wondered whether the sauce would still work with onion bits of every size.

Nevaeh had thought that sounded backwards at the time. Now her toes, all ten of them uncut, made a pretty good argument for it.

She picked the knife up carefully, washed it, and got back to work. The anonymous recipe said to cook the onion slowly until it turned soft and golden, so she lowered the heat and gave the sauce time, stirring it now and then, tasting, adding a pinch of sugar when it tasted sharp. Her mom drifted through the kitchen and peered over her shoulder. "Smells like somebody's nurturing that pot," she said, and Nevaeh laughed, because that was exactly what it felt like, patience and attention and the willingness to keep showing up.

When the pasta was drained and the sauce ladled over the top, her brother took one bite, then another, then a third without saying a word. Nevaeh watched him, spoon paused halfway to her own mouth. He looked up. "Can you make this again tomorrow?"

story:
Simon had been at Camp Windy Ridge for exactly six days, and he already knew which kids mattered and which kids got laughed at. He knew because at lunch on Tuesday, a boy named Marcus had tripped on the dock, dropped his tray into the lake, and three kids from Cabin 4 had howled like it was the funniest thing that had ever happened. Simon had watched. He had even smiled a little, because it did look funny, and then he had felt the smile go sour in his mouth when Marcus walked away with his head down.

The next morning, Ms. Yilmaz gathered the whole camp under the big oak by the mess hall for their weekly talk. She was building a wind turbine with the campers that week, and Simon liked her because she never gave speeches longer than two minutes. Today she wrote two words on her clipboard and held it up: BYSTANDER and UPSTANDER. "An upstander," she said, "is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander." Then she said, "Think about which one you were this week. We'll talk at the turbine build."

Simon thought about it all through the morning. He thought about it while his group tested blades in the creek, and while Milla explained, for the fourth time, that the plastic blades needed to decompose their shapes in her sketchbook before she could cut them, which made no sense until she drew it and he saw she meant breaking the shape into parts. Mostly he thought about Marcus. Being a bystander, he realized, was the thing he had done. The problem was what to do about it now, because yelling at Cabin 4 would just make them louder, and tattling to a counselor might make it worse for Marcus after the counselors left.

He tested a small idea at dinner. Marcus sat alone at the end of a table, so Simon slid his tray down across from him and asked how the kayak lesson had gone. That was all. Marcus looked up like a bird checking for hawks, then said the water had been cold and he'd tipped twice. Simon said he'd tipped three times. It wasn't much, but Cabin 4's loudest kid, Dev, watched them and said nothing.

On Thursday, Dev started up again at the dock, calling Marcus "Tray Dropper" in a voice like something corrosive, eating away at the quiet. Simon's heart banged. Alexis got his first phone on a Tuesday, and by Friday he had a rule for it: the phone stayed on his nightstand while he scrolled in bed. For three nights in a row he lay in the dark watching videos until eleven, then stared at the ceiling until nearly one, wide awake. He knew he wasn't nervous about anything, and he hadn't drunk any cola after dinner, so he started making a list on paper. The only thing that changed on the bad nights was the phone.

At school he described the pattern to Jordan, who yawned through half of it. "My mom calls it melatonin," Jordan said. "It's the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening. She says the light from screens can hold it back." Alexis wrote the word down. He didn't like taking an explanation from Jordan, of all people, who once claimed that microwave ovens worked by blowing hot air from the bottom.

He decided to test it. On Monday he left the phone in the kitchen after dinner and read a paper book in bed instead. He was asleep before ten thirty, which he only knew because he remembered turning his clock around and nothing after that. On Tuesday he scrolled in bed again until eleven and lay awake until almost one, listening to the furnace tick. On Wednesday, phone in the kitchen again, asleep fast. He did the same thing twice more that week, alternating like he was running some random experiment instead of just going to bed, and the pattern held every single time.

The twist came on Saturday. He explained the whole thing to his mother, expecting her to be impressed by his method, and she laughed. "That's why I keep my phone in the kitchen," she said. "I've done it for years." Alexis felt his face go hot, a flash of embarrassment at having discovered, with graphs and everything, a fact that had been taped to their household forever. He had assumed she was just terrible at charging her phone.

"So you're not getting rid of it?" Jordan asked on Monday. Alexis had already changed his mind about that. He liked the phone too much to give it up, and he didn't think he should have to.

"No," Alexis said. "I'm keeping it downstairs after dinner. It's not the phone, it's where I use it." That evening he plugged it into the kitchen outlet next to his mother's, and the two phones stood side by side in the dark, charging.

story:
Keira's problem was simple: she needed to see the cells of an onion skin, and she had exactly one afternoon to do it. Mr. Ma, who ran the community garden and let kids use the old microscope in his tool shed, had left a note taped to the door because he was at the dentist.

"Keira," the note read, "microscope is on the bench. Onion from the bed by the fence. Don't let the invasive mint near the vegetable beds, it takes over everything. If you get stuck, read the index card in the drawer. Mr. Ma."

She peeled a paper-thin layer from the onion, dropped it on a slide, and clamped it under the clips. Then she turned the big wheel until the longest lens, the one that looked most powerful, hovered right above the sample. Surely the strongest lens would show the most. She pressed her eye to the eyepiece.

Nothing. A gray blur, like looking through a shower door. She moved the slide left, right, forward, back. Still blur. She checked that the onion was actually there. It was, pale and delicate, mocking her.

Aris banged in with a watering can. "You look like you're fighting that microscope."

"It's winning," Keira said. "I can't find anything. It's just fog."

"Maybe you're too close," Aris said, and went to water the tomatoes.

Too close. Keira stared at the three lenses rotating on the nosepiece, short, medium, and long. The long one must magnify the most, but maybe it magnified the blur too. She pulled open the drawer and found Mr. Ma's index card, expecting a lecture in handwriting. Instead it said: "Lowest power first. Always."

She swung the shortest lens into place, looked through, and turned the wheel slowly. Shapes drifted up out of the fog, dozens of them, bricks in a wall, each with a dark dot near its middle. Cells. Actual cells. She switched to the medium lens, focused again, and there they were, bigger and clearer, the outline of each cell thick and definite, with the nucleus sitting inside like a stamp.

"Calla's going to lose her mind," she said. "She said onions were boring."

She grabbed a pencil and scrawled on the back of Mr. Ma's note: "Calla. Onion cells look like a brick wall, each one with a dot in the middle. Come see tomorrow. Bring snacks. Keira."

Then she labeled her drawing, wall, membrane, nucleus, and wanted to verify it, so she carried the slide outside to compare the drawing with the real thing. The onion in the bed looked smooth and secret, giving away nothing. Only the microscope knew. She held the slide up to the sun, and the little gray layer glowed like a window.

Lauren had the folded page from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in her jacket pocket, and she had read Section 3 so many times she could almost recite it: every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in elections for members of the House of Commons or of a legislature. Almost. In the crowded town hall, she kept sneaking looks at the paper while the council hashed out the town budget for the new arena roof.

Mr. Nakamura, who ran the hardware store and lived on her street, leaned over. "You're here for the roof vote too?"

"It's for Mr. Nakamura's, I mean, for class," she said, flustered. "We have to pick a right from the Charter and explain it in our own words at a town hall meeting. But mine keeps sounding like I copied it."

"Give it a try on me," he said.

Lauren straightened up. "Section 3 says every Canadian citizen can vote in elections for the House of Commons or a provincial legislature." Her voice got smaller. "See? Copied."

Across the aisle, Travis and Heidi were waving at her from the folding chairs near the front, where a table displayed sample ballots from the last federal election. A big cardboard sign above it read: VOTING IS OPEN TO CANADIAN CITIZENS. Lauren squinted at it, and a question formed. Why citizens? She scanned the crowd and spotted the cashier from the Thai cuisine place on Main Street, the one whose grandmother had moved from Bangkok and wasn't a citizen yet. If the grandmother couldn't vote, then the sign and Section 3 matched exactly. That was the test. If the rule were something else, like age or living here, the sign would say that instead.

She squeezed past knees to the front and tapped the election clerk on the shoulder. "Excuse me. If someone's a permanent resident but not a citizen, can they vote in the federal election?"

"No, hon. Citizens only."

Lauren walked back, feeling the pieces click. The rule wasn't about who lived here or who paid taxes toward the budget; it was about citizenship, and it stretched from the national House of Commons all the way down to the provincial legislatures. Not the town council, though. That was a separate thing, which was odd, and she filed it away.

When the meeting opened for questions, her hand went up before she could talk herself out of it. "I'm Lauren, from Grade seven, and I'm learning to explain one of our rights. Here's my own words version. In Canada, if you're a citizen, you get a say in picking who makes the laws, both in Ottawa and in your province. That's Section 3." Some people clapped, and Heidi whooped loud enough that the mayor raised an eyebrow.

Afterward the cashier came over, smiling. "My grandmother passed her citizenship test last month. Next election will be her first vote ever."

Lauren grinned and pulled out her pencil. "Can I write that down for my presentation?"

story:
Emilia unfolded her notebook on the picnic table, right beside the cake with thirteen candles still waiting to be lit. It was her birthday, but she had also called a meeting of the Nature Club, because today she was the president, and presidents, she had decided, needed agendas.

Felix groaned. "It's a party."

"It's a working party," Emilia said. "Item one: the creek cleanup. Item two: the birdhouse fund."

Evelina slid into the seat across from her and stole a cookie. "Can I talk about the creek? Because I have, like, a whole plan."

"Go ahead," Emilia said, and she wrote Evelina's plan on the agenda: gloves, trash bags, a poster, snacks proportional to the number of volunteers, more people meant more granola bars.

Then Felix raised his hand. "I move that we build a frog pond behind the gym."

"A what?" Evelina said.

"A frog pond. It's called a motion," Felix said. "It's a formal proposal for the club to do something."

Emilia remembered, suddenly, the last meeting, back in October, when Marcus had proposed a bake sale and they had argued about it for forty minutes. Forty minutes, and in the end only Marcus had even wanted it. She had gone home that night wondering why the whole meeting had gotten stuck on one person's idea. Now, watching Felix grin across the table, she had a suspicion, like a pattern clicking into place. Maybe the problem wasn't the idea. Maybe the problem was that nobody else supported it.

She flipped to the back of her notebook, where she'd copied the club's battered old rulebook, Robert's Rules, the one Ms. Sharma kept on the shelf above the aquarium. She ran her finger down the page and found it. "Under Robert's Rules," she read, "most motions need another member to second them before discussion begins."

"So," Emilia said slowly, testing the concept out loud, "if nobody seconds your frog pond, we don't debate it. We just move on."

Evelina blinked. "That's it? We can skip it?"

"Raise your hand if you second the frog pond," Emilia said.

Silence. A bee buzzed over the cake. Felix's grin wobbled.

"No second," Emilia said, and she drew a neat little line through item zero, which hadn't even made the agenda. Then came the twist: Evelina raised her hand. "Wait. I second it."

Felix straightened up like a plant given water. "Really?"

"Not a pond behind the gym. But a tiny one, in a bucket, for the science fair. If we modify the motion."

Emilia considered. A smaller frog pond, seconded, discussed for ten minutes instead of forty, voted on and passed, three to zero. She wrote it at the bottom of the agenda and underlined it twice.

Later, after the candles were blown out and the plates held nothing but crumbs, Felix leaned over her notebook. "Can I keep the agenda page?"

"Why?"

He tapped the crossed-out line. "Proof that my idea survived you."

"You almost didn't survive yourself," Evelina said, and stole his last cookie.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
story:
Aurora had agreed to explain the seasons in front of Mr. Demir's class on Monday, which had seemed like a fine idea on Thursday and a terrible one by Saturday afternoon. She sat on the porch of her grandmother's house with a flashlight, an orange, and a marker-drawn line around the orange's middle, because you could not exactly drag the solar system indoors.

Her grandmother came out with two glasses of lemonade and watched her tilt the orange and shine the flashlight at it. "That's an odd way to eat fruit," she said.

"I'm learning the tilt of Earth's axis," Aurora said. "The axis is this line through the middle. It stays tilted the same way while Earth goes around the Sun, so sometimes the north half leans toward the light and sometimes it leans away. That's the seasons." She moved the orange around the flashlight in a slow circle, keeping the marker line tilted. It was starting to make sense to her, which was suspicious, because it had not made sense all week.

She remembered Wednesday in class, when she had raised her hand and said summer happened because Earth was closer to the Sun. Micah had said "then why is it winter in Australia when it's summer here?" and Hayley had drawn a terrible picture of Earth on fire, and Mr. Demir had just said "test it," which was apparently how adults answered questions when they wanted you to suffer. So here she was, testing it, at her grandmother's, because her own house was full of little cousins.

The flashlight experiment had one flaw: it showed the tilt, but it did not prove anything about distance, and Aurora wanted proof. When she held the orange closer to the flashlight, the whole thing got brighter, top and bottom together. Closer made everything warmer, all at once, both halves. That was not what seasons did. Seasons took turns. So distance could not be what governed them, and she wrote that in her notebook with some satisfaction, then crossed out "governed" because it sounded like a word from a documentary, then wrote it again because she liked it.

Her grandmother disappeared inside and came back with a shoebox of photographs, most of them of people Aurora did not recognize and one of them of a man standing by a lake at what looked like sunset. "Your great-uncle took that north of the Arctic Circle," her grandmother said. "In June. He swore the clock said midnight when he took it."

Aurora held the photo under the porch light. The Sun sat low near the horizon, yellow and whole, above a lake that should have been dark. "The Sun. At midnight," she said.

"Stays up like that for at least one full day around the June solstice," her grandmother said. "They call it the midnight sun."

Aurora set down her lemonade. She tilted the orange hard, much more than Earth's real tilt, and walked it around the flashlight, watching the top half. The whole top half, even the far side of it, stayed lit at once when the tilt leaned in far enough. The pole never rolled into shadow. If the Sun could hang over one spot in the middle of the night, then the tilt was not just decoration. It could grab light and hold it there for a day. She got a fresh orange and drew a new axis line, and her grandmother leaned in over her shoulder.

"Am I the Sun or the flashlight?" her grandmother asked.

"You're the jury," Aurora said, and shone the light.

story:
The trumpet had beaten Brody eleven times in a row, and it was starting to feel personal. Every time he reached measure twenty, his fingers tripped over the same four notes, and the sound that came out was less like music and more like a goose being stepped on.

"It's getting worse," said Jack, who sat next to him in fourth-period band and had the merciful habit of saying exactly what everyone was thinking. "Yesterday it was a startled goose. Today the goose has opinions."

"Thanks, Jack."

"I'm just saying. Mr. Flores is going to hear that on Friday."

Friday was the problem. The winter concert was Friday at seven o'clock, three days away, and Mr. Flores had made it very clear that anyone who could not play the piece competently would be sitting in the audience instead of on stage, holding programs for people who could. Brody did not want to hand out programs. Handing out programs was the band room's way of humiliating you slowly, with a smile.

His plan had been simple: play the whole song over and over until the goose notes disappeared. He had played it twenty-two times that week. The goose notes remained, honking at measure twenty like they paid rent there. Meanwhile Dallas, who sat on the other side of him and had started the semester barely able to find her mouthpiece, was somehow getting better every single day. That made no sense. He practiced more than she did. He had counted.

So during Thursday practice, instead of playing, he watched her. She didn't run the whole piece either. She'd play a chunk, stop, squint at the sheet like it owed her money, then play the same small chunk again, slower, then faster, then snap her fingers and move on. She never once played the whole song start to finish. She just hunted down the spots where she messed up and worked on those until they surrendered.

"You're staring," Dallas said without looking up.

"You're doing it wrong. You're supposed to play the whole thing."

She shrugged. "My cousin did this violin thing where they studied people who are really good at stuff. The way you practice matters more than how many times you play the whole piece. You're supposed to go after the exact spots you keep missing." She tapped her music. "I miss measures twelve to sixteen, so I only play measures twelve to sixteen. It's boring, but it works."

Brody looked down at his sheet. Measures nineteen to twenty-three. Four measures. He had played the whole song twenty-two times, which meant he had actually practiced his weak spot twenty-two times while playing everything else four hundred times. No wonder the rest of the song sounded competent and those four measures sounded like an accident.

He raised his trumpet and played only measures nineteen through twenty-three. Goose. Again, slower. Less goose. Again. A small honk. Again. He was about to try it one more time when the thermostat on the wall clicked and the radiator by the window began to tick heat into the room, so loudly that Mr. Flores looked up from his desk.

"Brody, everything all right over there?"

"Measures twenty to twenty-three," Brody said. "That's all I'm doing until they're perfect."

Mr. Flores smiled and went back to his paperwork, and Jack leaned over. "Twenty to twenty-three? You skipped nineteen."

"I know," Brody said, and raised the trumpet again. "Nineteen was just lonely."

story:
The morning after their first real practice, Easton could barely walk down the stairs without grabbing the railing. At the rink that afternoon, Clarke flopped onto the bench beside him and groaned. "It's all that lactic acid," Clarke said, pulling his skate guard off with a wince. "Ms. Brennan was talking about it in science last year. It builds up when you work hard."

Easton laced his skates slowly, thinking. He could accept that his legs burned during the hard skating drills yesterday. That burn had faded before he even got in the car. This was different. This pain had shown up this morning, a full day later, deep in his thighs like someone had tightened every muscle with a wrench. He didn't say anything yet, because Clarke sounded certain and Easton didn't want to assume he was right when Clarke might be. But the timing bothered him. A burn that ends quickly couldn't be the same thing as a pain that starts a day late. Could it?

During the water break, he pulled Siena aside near the parallel bars where the little kids practiced. "Can I borrow your phone? Two minutes, I promise." He typed carefully, thumbs cold, and read until Siena leaned over his shoulder to see what was so interesting. "Delayed muscle soreness," he said quietly. "It's what we've got. And get this, lactic acid goes back to normal within about an hour after you stop exercising. Not a day. An hour." Siena raised her eyebrows. "So Clarke's blaming the wrong thing?" "Basically," Easton said, and pocketed the phone when the coach blew the whistle.

He decided to test it, in his own small way. That night he wrote a note and left it on the fridge where his dad would find it: "Doing 40 squats at 7 p.m. Check my legs at 8, then again tomorrow morning. For science. Signed, Easton." At eight his father poked his thigh and reported nothing, no burn, no soreness. Easton went to bed almost disappointed. At 6:30 the next morning, though, he woke to legs that felt like solid wood, and he limped to the kitchen grinning through the ache. The burn was long gone; the soreness had arrived on schedule, a day late.

At Thursday's practice he sat down next to Clarke with his skates already on. "Hey, about the lactic acid," he said. "I looked it up, and I did squats to check. That stuff's back to normal within about an hour after you exercise. Our sore legs are something else, delayed muscle soreness. It's normal, and it means we worked hard." Clarke rubbed his thigh, considering, then shrugged. "Okay, but if it's normal, why does it feel like my legs hate me?" Easton laughed and grabbed his stick. "Come on, Coach has us doing suicide sprints in five minutes."

Grandpa's house smelled like sawdust and burnt coffee, and Aria had claimed the porch swing as her homework spot because the Wi-Fi reached it and nobody else wanted it. The list was getting embarrassing. story:
Eva sat on the low wall by the swings, her left arm in a bright green cast, watching the other kids line up for the monkey bars. She could not climb, could not even push herself off the wall properly, so she had made a plan instead: figure out what her cast actually was. Three days ago she had fallen off the climbing rope, and she still remembered the sickening snap, then the long ride to the hospital while her mom drove and repeated "almost there, almost there." The doctor had wrapped her arm in wet, soggy strips that smelled like a chalkboard, and by the time they got home those strips had turned hard as a shell.

"It's plaster of Paris," Kayson had said that morning, squinting at the cast. "Sehaj told me. But what did people do before casts existed? Just... lie in bed forever?"

"That can't be right," Eva said. "Soldiers broke bones all through history. Somebody had to fix them." At lunch she and Sehaj found a bench near the fence, out of the way of the soccer game, and Sehaj pulled out the library book he had checked out for her, since Eva could only turn pages with one hand. He held it open while she scanned the page about broken bones.

"There," Eva said, tapping the paragraph with her good hand. "Listen to this." Sehaj read aloud, and the fact landed like a small treasure: "Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852." Sehaj frowned. "A surgeon? For the army?"

"Think about it," Eva said. "Soldiers fall off horses and get trampled. He probably saw so many broken arms that he needed something fast and hard. And 1852 is not that long ago. That means before then, nobody had this." She looked down at her green shell. "My arm is basically the same idea he had. Only his weren't green."

"So how do you know the book is right?" Sehaj asked. "Maybe it made a mistake."

Eva had been wondering the same thing, and she had a test ready. Plaster was the stuff teachers used to fill holes in walls, and Ms. Fraser kept a small bucket of it in the art room for making molds. At recess the next day, Ms. Fraser let Eva dip a strip of bandage into the wet plaster, just once and carefully, and Eva laid the soggy strip across a paper cup. It sagged and looked useless. "Watch," Eva whispered, mostly to herself. Twenty minutes later, while the soccer ball thumped and someone shrieked about a goal, she pressed the strip. Hard. Curved exactly like the cup, like a little white bridge.

"1852," Sehaj said, poking it. "That's the same stuff."

"Told you," Eva said, and held it up in the sun, turning her good hand so the light caught it.

Julia slid the photocopied diary pages across the library table and frowned at them again. "This is never going to tell me anything," Julia said.

Jemma looked up from her own stack of documents. "You just have to persevere. Read it like a detective, not like a book."

"That's a consequence," Jemma said slowly. "They went too early."

"Right," she said. "Next time." She slid the diary pages back into her folder, on top of the encyclopedia volume she still hadn't returned.

He decided to test it. At dinner he set a bowl of sunflower seeds next to his father's plate, the kind his father crunched during football games, and he said nothing about vaping or withdrawal or any of it. His father ate the seeds slowly, then a second handful, and by the time Michael cleared the plates, his father had asked two whole questions about the reward pathway poster and even suggested a diagram. It wasn't a cure, but it was a pattern, and Michael had seen it work.

The next morning Michael asked his father to drive him to school early so he could set up. In the car his father gripped the wheel and admitted, "I quit cold turkey. It's harder than I thought. I owe you an apology."

"Withdrawal," Michael said. "It's not you, it's the nicotine leaving."

At school, Mr. Hu was stacking chairs, and Michael asked whether he could add one more slide to his presentation, a real example. Then he called Mathis over to hold the poster while he taped on a photograph of the aquarium, blue and bright against the white board.

story:
Natalie spread her supplies across the library table: a pencil, a roll of tracing paper, and the flyer for the library's anonymous postcard contest. The rules said entrants could not sign their names, which suited her fine. She wanted her art judged on its own, not on who made it. She had chosen a design of a compass rose made entirely of tiny pencil-drawn stars.

She had barely started when a boy from her street slid into the seat across from her. He was eight, and he was holding his hand up like he'd been burned. "I poked myself," he said. "With a pencil. Am I going to get lead poisoning?"

"You washed it?" Natalie asked. He nodded. "Then you're fine." He didn't look convinced. He kept staring at the small gray smudge on his palm, and Natalie could see that telling him to calm down would only obstruct the conversation rather than help it. Eight-year-olds needed proof.

She remembered something from a book she'd read here last year, something about pencils, and she wasn't sure she had it right. She raised her hand toward the reference desk, and Ms. Tremblay came over. Natalie asked where the books on pencils and drawing materials would be, without mentioning the boy, and Ms. Tremblay pointed her to a shelf near the window. Ms. Tremblay had a way of answering the question you asked instead of the one you were really asking, which was exactly the compassion Natalie needed at that moment.

Natalie pulled a thin book about the history of drawing tools and found the page in under a minute. She read it twice, then carried it back. "Okay," she said, setting the book between them. "Pencil lead has never contained the metal lead. It's graphite." The boy frowned at the word. "The black stuff in your pencil. People used to mistake graphite for a kind of lead ore, and the name stuck. So there's no lead in there at all. Nothing to poison you."

The boy looked at the page, then at his palm, then at the book again. "Never?" he asked. "Not even a little?"

"Not even a little," Natalie said. He wiped his hand on his jeans anyway, and then, reassured, he leaned over her postcard and told her that one of her compass points was crooked. She checked it against the edge of the table. He was right. She erased the star and redrew it.
