activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
story:
Alexandra stood in the humid kitchen with her speech cards fanned across the counter, rehearsing for the fourth time. On Monday she had to give a five-minute talk in front of her whole history class, and Mr. Moretti had asked for two volunteers to be candidates for the regional speech contest. She had raised her hand before she thought it through, and now her heart hammered every time she pictured the room.

Courtney came through the back door with Nyla behind her, both of them still carrying their gym bags. "You look like you're about to be sick," Courtney said, dropping her bag on a chair.

"I'm fine," Alexandra said, which was obviously not true. Her hands were shaking enough that the cards rattled.

Nyla picked up one of the cards and read it. "You've got anxiety written in the margin. Twice."

"That's my mom's word. She's been saying I need coping skills, not just more practice runs in the kitchen." Alexandra squared the cards. "But she's at work and I don't actually have any."

Nyla sat down. "My brother's a goalie. He does this thing before penalty shots. He breathes out slow, longer than the breath in, like he's fogging a window with one long stream. He says everybody on his team does it before a stressful moment because slow breathing with long exhales calms the body's stress response. It's the most boring trick in the world and it works."

Alexandra tried it right there. In for three counts, out until her lungs felt empty, the kitchen air warm and damp around her. After the fourth exhale her hands had stopped rattling the cards. She read the opening line and her voice came out level.

"Okay," Courtney said. "Now set a boundary with yourself. One more run-through, then you stop for the night. My mom says rehearsing past midnight just makes it worse."

"One more," Alexandra agreed. She set the timer on the stove, breathed out slow and long, and started at the top. When she finished, Nyla was holding up a score card made from a napkin that said ten, and Alexandra laughed and dealt the cards onto the counter like a magician.

"Monday," she said, and exhaled again, slow and long.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
Muhammad set the microscope on the picnic table in the backyard, careful to keep it in the shade of the umbrella so the sun wouldn't glare through the lens. Ms. Rivera, his neighbour and a retired lab technician, had lent it to him for the weekend along with a box of slides, a bottle of stain, and a note that read, in her neat handwriting, "Onions are patient teachers." His friend Jad had already claimed the second chair, and Marilyn sat cross-legged on the grass with a purple onion in her lap like a small cannonball.

"Ms. Rivera says we have to see the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus," Muhammad said, unfolding the diagram she had photocopied for him. "And label all three."

Jad peeled a layer of skin off the onion while Muhammad fetched a cup of water from the kitchen. His mother was at the doctor's getting a prescription refilled, so the backyard belonged entirely to the three of them and the wasp that kept circling the lemonade. Marilyn laid the thin slice of skin on the slide with tweezers, added a drop of stain, and then lowered the coverslip flat, straight down, like a lid on a pot.

Under the lowest magnification, the field of view filled with round shapes, dark-ringed and scattered everywhere. "Those are the cells," Marilyn said, turning the fine focus. "Look, they're everywhere. That was easy."

Muhammad leaned in and looked for a long moment. Something bothered him. The shapes had no edges that met, no neat rows like the diagram, and each one was a perfect circle with a thick black ring. "Cells have straight sides in the picture," he said slowly. "These are round. And they're all different sizes, even in the same spot." He straightened up. "I don't think those are cells. I think they're bubbles. Air bubbles."

Marilyn lifted the coverslip off, tilted the slide toward the light, and squinted. "Then where are the cells?"

"Under the bubbles, maybe. Or squished somewhere." Muhammad thought about the coverslip. When Marilyn had dropped it flat, it must have trapped air underneath. He looked at the next blank slide, then picked up the tweezers with a fresh piece of onion skin. "Let's try putting it down at an angle, one edge first, and lowering it slowly."

Jad supervised the drop of stain, holding the dropper steady while Muhammad touched the edge of the coverslip to the liquid and let it fall in a slow hinge. "Keep going," Jad said. "Nice and easy." Muhammad lowered it until it lay flat, and not one circle rose up under the glass.

Marilyn looked first. She was quiet for a second, then said, "Muhammad. Come look."

The field of view was full of rectangles, brick-shaped and fitted together in tidy rows, each with a darker outline. Muhammad turned to the higher magnification and focused until a small dense spot appeared near the centre of one cell. "That's the nucleus," he said. "And the dark outline is the wall. The membrane is right inside it, thin, like a second edge." He pulled the diagram close and printed the three labels in pencil beside his drawing, then drew a fourth label with an arrow pointing at nothing: "bubbles, gone."

Ms. Rivera came out to take back her lemonade pitcher that evening and peered through the eyepiece. She was quiet in her neutral, careful way, and then she said, "Brick wall. Textbook quality."

"Angle first," Muhammad told her, holding up the slide. "One edge, then down slow."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
Jeremy stared at his laptop screen, where his short story had exactly one paragraph of glory: the dragon attacked the castle, the knight won, the end. It had taken him twenty minutes, and it was terrible, though he couldn't say why. Something about it felt like eating one potato chip and being handed the bill.

He called Ty, who showed up at the back door ten minutes later with a bag of chips, which felt like a personal insult. "Read this," Jeremy said, sliding the laptop across the kitchen table. Ty read it, chewing. Then he read it again, slower, which was a bad sign. "The dragon's cool," Ty offered. "But I don't care if the knight wins. It's like you fast-forwarded to the good part and skipped the movie."

"The good part is the point," Jeremy said. "It's the climax. Mr. Villanueva kept saying that word like it was a trophy." He flipped through his notebook, where he'd written the assignment in his neatest handwriting: dialogue correctly punctuated, clear climax, and something called rising action, underlined twice because he'd copied it off the board in a hurry. He had allocated a whole evening to this story and had produced a paragraph that read like a fire alarm.

"So what's rising action?" Ty asked, stealing another chip. Jeremy lined up three more paragraphs in his head, an experiment. He started over: first the knight noticed the village milk cows going missing, one by one. Then he found a scale in the mud, wide as a dinner plate. Then a girl from the village insisted on coming along, and she argued with the knight about which road to take, and they took the wrong one, and night fell. Ty leaned in without seeming to notice he was doing it. "Predatory," Ty said, pointing at a line where the dragon watched the two of them from the ridge. "You should use that word. It's a good word." Jeremy typed it in, then added dialogue, checking each quotation mark against his notebook rules. "The girl gets a stake in it," he muttered. "The reader gets a reason to worry."

He read the new draft aloud, and when he reached the dragon's attack, Ty grabbed the chip bag and squeezed it until it crinkled like a sensor going off. "See, now it matters," Ty said. "It's rising action. Complications that build tension before the climax, that's what makes the big moment land." Jeremy saved the file twice, then a third time for luck, and pushed the laptop back toward his friend. "Okay, expert. Then you write the ending line of dialogue, and I'll check your commas." Ty cracked his knuckles over the keyboard like a tiny, chip-dusted dragon.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
story:
"It says right here that our town was founded in 1887," Emrick said, tapping the poster he'd made for history class. "Mr. Peters put it on the assignment sheet, so it has to be right."

Declan frowned at the poster. "My grandpa's plaque says 1892. That's five years different. One of them is wrong."

"Maybe your grandpa's plaque is wrong," Emrick said. "Teachers don't make stuff up."

Dahlia leaned over the table in the school library, where the three of them had spread out their project materials after last period. "My uncle says the town hall has a big sign with 1887 on it too," she offered. "So that's two against one."

Declan didn't like losing, but he liked guessing even less. "The plaque is old, though. Maybe older than the sign." He looked toward the front desk, where Ms. Oyelaran was stamping returned books. He'd been in trouble with her before over a chronic late-returns problem, so he walked over slowly. "Do we have any old newspapers here? Like from when the town started?"

She set down her stamp. "Back corner, the microfilm cabinet. And there's a shelf of the early bound volumes." She pointed. "Careful with the pages. They crumble."

Dahlia caught up to him in the corner. "You realize this is a paradox," she said. "You're doing extra research to prove the teacher wrong, and if you're wrong, you did all this for nothing."

"It's not a paradox if I find out either way," Declan said, pulling a fat volume off the shelf. The spine read 1887. He opened it gently. The pages smelled like dust and old rain.

The first issue lay flat in front of them. Emrick read the masthead out loud, quieter than usual. "'First edition, printed in our new town.'" The date under it was clear. 1887. Not 1892.

"That settles it," Emrick said. "The paper was printed here in 1887."

"No, it doesn't," Declan said. He turned pages carefully, scanning. "The paper proves the town had a printing shop then. But the plaque says founded, and founding might mean something different. Like the first settler, or the first store." He kept flipping. Near the back of the first volume he stopped. A letter to the editor, signed by an early settler, described arriving with her family years before the newspaper began and described the day the town was officially marked out and recorded. The details matched the plaque's story.

"Look," Declan said. "A firsthand record from the time. Someone who was actually there, writing it down when it happened. A letter like this is called a primary source."

Emrick crouched beside him and read the letter twice. "So the teacher's 1887 is when the paper started, and the plaque's 1892 is..." He stopped. "Wait, the letter says the town was marked out in the spring. Let me check that date again."

Dahlia was already photographing the page with her phone for their project. "You'd better advocate for the plaque in class tomorrow," she told Declan. "Bring the volume."

He carried it to the front desk with both hands, like something that could still break. "Ms. Oyelaran, can I take this to history class in the morning?"

She looked at the letter, then at him, and wrote his name on a slip. "Back by Friday."

"It'll be back tomorrow," Declan said, and tucked the slip into his pocket.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
story:
Lincoln had twenty-three dollars in his pocket and one plan: buy the Stormscale dragon plush at the mall before they sold out. The trouble started the moment he reached the toy store, where a line curved past the fountain and a worker was dismantling the window display, pulling the very last dragons off their perches. "Sold out in forty minutes," the worker said. Lincoln's stomach dropped like an elevator with a cut cable.

Outside the food court, a boy from his grade named Mehtab sat behind a folding table with six Stormscale dragons lined up in a neat row. A sign read forty dollars each. "You bought them all," Lincoln said. "The store sells them for fifteen." Mehtab shrugged. "People are paying forty. Watch." A man in a Running Is My Cardio shirt bought two without even blinking.

Lincoln didn't have forty dollars, so he watched instead. A woman offered thirty, and Mehtab held firm. A kid offered twenty-five, and Mehtab still said no. Then a girl named Anna-Eve walked up, counted her money, and said, "I've got thirty-two." Mehtab looked at his row of dragons, which hadn't shrunk in an hour, and said, "Deal." After that the buyers came faster, and the table emptied one dragon at a time until only one was left, and Mehtab let that one go for twenty-eight.

"You lowered the price," Lincoln said. "Why?" Mehtab stacked his empty display box. "Mr. Francis explained it to my sister for her economics curriculum. The price where buyers want exactly as many as the seller has is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price. It's the price that clears you out." He grinned. "Forty cleared me out of nothing."

Lincoln turned that over while he waited for his mom outside the bookstore. He had seen the whole thing without knowing there was a name for it. High price, no buyers. Lower price, dragons gone. It was like the mall escalators running in parallel, each one carrying people in a steady stream, only this one carried dragons and dollars.

The next Saturday he came back with his twenty-three dollars. The store had restocked, and a new shipment sat stacked in a bin beside a sign reading fifteen dollars, no limit. Two boys walked right past the bin toward the food court, where Mehtab's table stood empty except for a folded sign. Lincoln picked up a dragon, paid the cashier, and held it under his arm like a trophy.

"Stormscale number two?" the cashier asked.

"Number one," Lincoln said. "I just got him the honest way."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
story:
Rebecca's flight to visit her grandmother was delayed three hours, which meant she had three hours to learn something she had promised her grandmother she understood: the monsoon. Grandmother grew rice on a small plot, and on the video call last Sunday she had asked, "Do you know what water my rice drinks in summer?" Rebecca had said yes. That was a lie, and it had been sitting in her stomach ever since. She spread her geography book across two seats at the gate while her dad went to buy tea, and beside her, her classmate Elly, who happened to be on the same flight, leaned over her shoulder.

"That arrow's weird," Elly said, poking the weather map on Rebecca's screen. The map showed India in green and gray, and a fat red arrow pointed at the coast from the ocean below and to the left. "Why does it point from the sea? Weather comes from the sky, not sideways."

Rebecca stared at the arrow. The map labeled the ocean the Arabian Sea, and the arrow came up from the lower left, which she knew from the compass rose in the corner was the southwest. Wind had a direction, she realized, the same way a river did, and you could read where it came from by which way the arrow's tail stretched. She rotated the book so the arrow pointed toward Elly. "Wind blows from somewhere," she said slowly. "This one comes from the southwest, across that sea. It's carrying water. Look, the whole southwest coast is dark blue."

Elly frowned at the screen. "So all that rain on the map, the rice part, is sea water that flew?" She said it like a joke, but Rebecca was already flipping pages. The chapter had one sentence she'd skipped before, and now it made sense: India's summer monsoon is called the southwest monsoon because its moist winds blow in mostly from the southwest, across the Arabian Sea. "That's its name," she told Elly, tapping the sentence. "The southwest monsoon." Elly repeated the name the way she repeated vocabulary words before a quiz, and Rebecca felt the thing in her stomach loosen.

"I want to check something," she said. She walked to the big departure board, Elly trailing behind, and found the flights from Mumbai and Kochi, cities on that same southwest coast. Every one was marked delayed in red, and one was cancelled. A tired man beside them with a rolling suitcase said the airport had been getting vigorous rain all afternoon, and that planes could handle rain but not the flooding on the coastal runways. Rebecca copied the delayed city codes into her notebook. It wasn't a science experiment, exactly, but it was a pattern, and patterns were how you believed something you couldn't see. Wind you couldn't see; water in the air you couldn't see; but delayed flights, you could see.

Her dad came back with tea and an extra cup for Elly, who always got cold in air conditioning, and he had adjusted the vent above their seats to regulate the draft so it wouldn't blow straight on her. Elly wrapped both hands around the cup and asked what the plane's shiny skin was made of, and Rebecca, still reading, answered without looking up, "Aluminum alloy, probably. Some mix of metals." She wrote one last note, about rice fields needing the summer rain, and drew the arrow again from memory, tail in the sea, head on the coast. Then she took out her phone and dialed her grandmother, because the monsoon could explain itself better in her own words than in a copied sentence. "The wind comes from the sea," she said when the call connected. "From the southwest, over the Arabian Sea. And now I know why your rice is green."
